## 2. Symbol Analysis

**1. The Spiritual Number 13:**

The number 13 has always been associated with death, endings, and transformation.

In the West, it is considered an unlucky number that people avoid.

But when viewed together with the Death card in the Tarot, 13 is not a curse at all; it is one of the universe’s laws—an ending that makes way for rebirth.

- **Inevitable Ending and Reorganization**

13 follows 12—12 represents completion, the zodiac’s twelve signs, and Heracles’ twelve labors culminating in his deification.

**13 symbolizes an irresistible ending.**

The Death rides a white horse, emotionless and indifferent to status; even a king kneeling and begging is futile.

This is not punishment but inevitability—

Rigid patterns, exhausted relationships, outdated beliefs, no matter how reluctant you are, must be let go.

Because without “death,” there can be no “life.”

This is actually a violent reorganization.

Like the “blackening” phase in alchemy: everything old is shattered and dissolved to extract new essence.

The process is painful, but the soul’s evolution is never gentle or easy.

![Tarot illustration](https://internal-api-drive-stream.feishu.cn/space/api/box/stream/download/authcode/?code=YzZkNGRjMTliYzU2M2NhMTRhZWZlNzIwM2Q4MjM5ZThfOTZjOTAxZDA3MjNiN2NjNzY0MmY0M2E3ODA3M2ViNjBfSUQ6NzYxOTIzNDEwNjAxNDY4MjI5MF8xNzgyMTgxNDMzOjE3ODIyNjc4MzNfVjM)

- **13 Viewed as 1 and 3**

If you break down 13, it becomes more interesting.

12 is the end of the old world; after 13 comes 1—the start of a new world.

The Death card is exactly the 13th card in the Major Arcana, like a watershed:

Before it are the Hanged Man’s accumulation, trials, and pause;

After it are Temperance’s harmony, rebirth, and integration.

So the “destruction” of 13 is not a reset but a purification.

The remaining “1” is no longer the naive beginning,

but a clearer, more authentic self setting out anew after shedding illusions.



**2. Belongs to the Water Element**

Water has powerful dissolving and purifying abilities. Like the river in the distance on the card, symbolizing the River Styx, it represents the thorough washing away of old emotions, memories, or identities. This cleansing is not destruction but a clearing to make space for new things.

Water also symbolizes the flow of the subconscious. When the Death card appears, it often means that some deeply rooted emotional patterns or psychological habits are quietly changing within. This change may be invisible but, like flowing water, will eventually reshape your life’s direction—a subtle but profound transformation.



**3. Astrological Correspondence: Scorpio**

Scorpio’s theme is “death and rebirth”—it seeks not superficial adjustment but profound inner transformation. This perfectly matches the message of the Death card: only by ending the old can the new be born.

Scorpio’s energy is intense and irresistible, like the Death figure riding the white horse on the card, slowly approaching with unstoppable force. From the moment we are born, we are moving toward death. It reminds us that sometimes we must let go of control and follow life’s own rhythm. This power demands surrender and trust in life’s flow. True strength comes from letting go and trusting.



**4. Hebrew Letter: Nun**

In Kabbalistic mysticism, the Death card corresponds to the Hebrew letter Nun (נ), meaning “fish.” Fish live underwater, symbolizing hidden wisdom and deep life force. In many ancient cultures, fish are also associated with resurrection and regeneration.

Nun also implies the eternal cycle of life between “endings” and “beginnings.” Just as fish cannot live without water, life requires repeated “deaths” to be reborn.

## 3. Case Studies

## Death—Lin Pinru’s Powerful Return

Lin Pinru’s story is a textbook example of “Death’s arrival.”

She was pushed into the sea by her husband Hong Shixian and her best friend Aili, lost her unborn child, held a funeral, and had her identity erased.

Legally and socially, “Lin Pinru” was already dead.

This is the most literal death—not metaphorical but an official declaration of ending.

But the real death happened inside her heart.



She once believed marriage was a safe harbor, only to have the person beside her overturn the boat;

She regarded Aili as a sister, but was robbed of her husband, home, and life;

Losing her unborn child severed her attachment to the role of “gentle wife.”

Her emotional world collapsed; she no longer believed in love or expected justice.

Like the fallen woman beneath Death’s horse—emotional, dependent, naive—all buried together.



Then, she was reborn as “Gao Shanshan.”

She accepted Gao Wenyan’s rigorous training: learning to swim to face her fear of drowning, practicing golf, changing her accent, transforming her temperament;

She discarded her timid personality and grew sharp edges.

When she walked into the Hong family engagement party with cold confidence, even Hong Shixian didn’t recognize her.

She didn’t just “get stronger,” she killed the bullied version of herself.

This is the harshest and most merciful truth of the Death card:

You must die once to live as someone else.



Her return was both a revenge ritual and Death’s judgment.

Hong Shixian, Aili, and mother-in-law Bai Fengwan were all shocked—the old order was forcibly torn apart.

She was no longer a victim but the one controlling the whole situation.

Like Death stepping over the king and the pope, she crushed her former abusers with her new identity.



Her methods were ruthless—scheming, provoking, psychological warfare—but her motive was always clear:

To seek justice for her wrongfully lost child,

To expose the hypocrisy of marriage and friendship,

To reclaim her trampled dignity.

Her “evil” was awakened clarity and self-protection.

Her revenge was a compensation for justice’s absence—

Just as Death enforces the universe’s law of cause and effect.



And Death never promises “unscathed rebirth.”

Even after avenging her great wrongs, she could never return to the past:

She learned calculation but lost innocence;

She won victory but forever lost her child and pure love.

She could choose forgiveness, but she chose to guard this new identity for life—

Because “Lin Pinru” was dead; the one who lives on is Gao Shanshan.



Those around her faced this upheaval like the figures beneath Death’s horse:

Hong Shixian clung to nostalgia but feared the truth, ultimately collapsing—that was the king’s resistance;

Gao Wenyan silently supported her, witnessing her rebirth—that was the pope’s submission;

Aili went from arrogance to breakdown, refusing to admit Pinru was not dead—that was the woman’s denial;

And Hong Shixian and Aili’s child was innocently caught up but would inherit this karma—that was the child’s innocence.



Many only saw her “dark transformation,”

But overlooked Death card’s deepest mercy:

If she didn’t die, she would always be the trampled Lin Pinru;

If she didn’t kill her weakness, she couldn’t protect her future self.

Her revenge was never to destroy others,

But to reclaim agency,

To prove “I deserve respect,”

And to make those who hurt her see with their own eyes—

She was reborn from the fire, more inviolable than before.

This is the ultimate revelation of the Death card:

True rebirth is not returning to the past,

But building a stronger city on the ruins.



That day the waves pushed her ashore,

Death had quietly arrived.

Lin Pinru sank beneath the sea,

Gao Shanshan was reborn from the ashes.



She is not a vengeful ghost demanding lives,

But a mortal forced to become a god.

And the Death card in Tarot whispered a thousand years ago:

“Those who do not dare to kill their past will be killed by it;

Those who dare to bury themselves can be reborn from the ashes.”
